utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. I would like to invite the parties that whenever the team, the Prosecution and Defence is not complete, to report that to the Chamber at the beginning of every hearing. Although I will not ask every day for the appearances of both parties, would there be any additional member to the team, the Chamber would like this member to be introduced by the parties. First of all, I have to apologise for making a mistake at the end of the Pre-Trial Conference earlier held this afternoon. We did not return into open session when we were in private session. In order to let the public know what happened, I point out that after we had heard, as the last point on the agenda, some submissions in relation to the health of Mr. Krajisnik, that we -- the only thing we then did is to establish that neither party had anything further to submit, whereupon the Chamber has adjourned until the start of the trial at a quarter past 3.00, that is, this moment. We are about to start a trial which might keep us together for a very long period of time. That time is needed because of the complex and the serious factual and legal matters the case confronts us with. If no 98 bis motion will be filed at the end of the Prosecution case, or if such a motion would fail to be successful, the time this trial will take may well be over two years. I call upon the parties to be as efficient in this trial as possible, but I immediately add to that that this is not an invitation not to do whatever you have to do to fulfil your difficult tasks, and I'm addressing both Prosecution and Defence, to fulfil your task for the full hundred per cent. The experience the Chamber has gained in the pre-trial stage makes us confident that the parties will perform their duties to the best of their, I should say, great abilities, and also in a spirit appropriate for such a trial. The Chamber, although perhaps not as passive as usual in common-law systems is fully aware of the assistance it needs from the parties to also perform its duties and to make its determinations. After these few remarks, I'd like to turn to Rule 84 and 84 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Before presenting its evidence, the Prosecution and the Defence may make opening statements, and the Defence may make its statement after the conclusion of the case of the Prosecutor. The Chamber has understood that the Defence has elected not to make its opening statement at this very moment and to postpone that, I presume, until before the presentation of evidence for the Defence. After the opening statements, Mr. Krajisnik, after the opening statement in this case, of the Prosecution, you may, if you wish to do so and if the Trial Chamber would decide to allow you, make a statement, under the control of the Trial Chamber, but you'll not be compelled to make a solemn declaration and you'll not be examined about the contents of the statement. The Chamber has also understood that you prefer not to make such a statement after the opening statement of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I say straight away that although that was the preliminary indication at 65 ter, in fact Mr. Krajisnik does propose to make what will be a short statement, with the Tribunal's permission. It will be a matter of just a very few minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then it's good that at least I paid attention to Rule 84 bis, so that it's clear now that Mr. Krajisnik would like to make a short statement, and the Chamber will give its decision on whether the Chamber allows Mr. Krajisnik to do so. Having gone through the Rules, Mr. Harmon, the Prosecution may proceed to make its opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fabled Bosnia, with its rich history, diverse peoples and cultures, its ambiance of tolerance and respect, lay shattered and in ruins in 1992. This case will reveal how that happened. This case had its origins in the process of the disintegration of a state, Yugoslavia, and in the emergence of a new state, Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is a case about Bosnian Serb political leaders who resisted this process, insisting that their vision must prevail, and preferring to cast their lot and the lives and fortunes of their peoples on it rather than with the emerging new independent state. As the political tide swung away from the political vision, from their political vision of the state, and it became increasingly less likely that they would achieve their objectives, the Bosnian Serb political leaders increasingly resorted to the politics of fear, often invoking old historical grudges and wrongs to incite their people to violence against their neighbours. Their ethnocentric form of politics became the politics of separation, where the blood and the suffering of their enemies was viewed as the harsh, but necessary cost of achieving their dreams of a Serbian state. This is the trial of one of those political leaders, Momcilo Krajisnik. The man who sits in the dock in this courtroom was a politician, a shrewd and calculating man, a committed and unrepentant Serb nationalist, who, along with Radovan Karadzic was one of the chief policy-makers of the Bosnian Serbs, policies that ignited the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, policies that were implemented through massive, state-sponsored crimes, the scale of which have not been seen in Europe since the Second World War. These crimes fall under the rubric of ethnic cleansing, a modern term for crimes that have plagued humanity for ages; the killing, persecution, deportation and forcible transfer of people because of their race, religion, or national origin, the razing of entire villages and settlements, the destruction of religious sites. The accused is a well-educated man holding a master's degree in economics from the University of Sarajevo. He worked as an economist in various enterprises in the former Yugoslavia and was a man who, along with his friend Radovan Karadzic, entered the political arena late in life. When he entered politics, he joined the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, also known as the SDS, one of the nationalist parties that emerged in the tumultuous post-Tito era in that republic. Along with Radovan Karadzic, it was his hand which held firmly the levers of power and authority, reflected in the significant positions he held and cemented Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by his close relationship with Radovan Karadzic, the charismatic public face of the SDS. Working within the machinery of the SDS and later within the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Krajisnik was vital in developing and promoting ethnocentric policies that exploited fearsome shadows of the past, policies that were later implemented in Bosnia to cleanse non-Serbs from the territories claimed by the Serbs. In November of 1990 he was elected to the Chamber of Citizens as an SDS deputy from the electoral district of Sarajevo. The Chamber of Citizens was one of two chambers of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As a result of the interparty agreements that followed the elections, he became the president of the assembly, and he continued in that powerful position until there was a final rupture of relations between the ethnic parties on the issue of Bosnian sovereignty. Thereafter, the accused's leading role in the SDS was translated into top leadership positions in the newly created organs of the republic proclaimed by the Bosnian Serbs. On their path to ethnic separation, the SDS, in October of 1991, created a separate assembly of Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the accused was appointed its president, a position that he retained throughout the period of this indictment. On the 2nd of June, 1992, he became a member of the expanded presidency, the highest executive authority in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The expanded presidency was a collective decision-making body that exercised executive authority. As Radovan Karadzic explained the decision making process, and I quote him: "We put all ideas on the table, discussed them, and then we decide which is best. We go on." Along with other members of the expanded presidency, Radovan Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, Nikola Koljevic, and Branko Djeric, the accused decided on what was the best manner to implement his vision of an ethnically separated Bosnia and Herzegovina. Through his positions and influence in the SDS and the Bosnian Serb government, Momcilo Krajisnik was a paramount Bosnian Serb political figure whom we allege in the indictment is responsible for massive crimes committed in Bosnia and Herzegovina between the 1st of July, 1991 and the 30th of December, 1992. The criminal charges against Krajisnik that are contained in the indictment number eight: One count of genocide; one count of complicity in genocide; five counts of crimes against humanity, those being persecutions, extermination, murder, deportation, and inhumane acts; and one count of a violation of laws or customs of war, murder. We allege under each of those counts that Mr. Krajisnik is responsible both under Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of our Statute, and I will discuss that later in my remarks. Included in the indictment are four separate schedules, with each schedule representing a type of crime, location of municipality, a date where specific killings occurred, where specific killings occurred in detention facilities, where specific religious sites and cultural monuments were destroyed and where detention facilities were located. We allege in the indictment that Mr. Krajisnik is responsible for these crimes alleged in the indictment because he planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning or preparation of those crimes. Now, when I use the term "committed," I'm referring to his participation. Along with other individual in a joint criminal enterprise, the objective of which was the permanent removal, by force or other means, of Bosnian Muslim, Bosnian Croat, or other non-Serb inhabitants from large areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina claimed to be Serbian, through the commission of crimes. The crimes identified in the four separate schedules were within the objective of the joint criminal enterprise or were natural and foreseeable consequences of it. As one of the members of the criminal enterprise, Krajisnik was fully aware of the horrific consequences that its implementation would visit on non-Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was indifferent to them. Mr. Krajisnik did not participate in this joint criminal enterprise alone. He worked closely and in concert with others to achieve the objectives of the enterprise, including Radovan Karadzic, Nikola Koljevic, Biljana Plavsic, Slobodan Milosevic, Arkan, General Ratko Mladic, General Momir Talic, Radoslav Brdjanin and others whose names you will become familiar with during the course of this trial. Like Mr. Krajisnik, each member of the joint criminal enterprise participated in and contributed to the criminal enterprise in different ways. Now, to fully understand the crimes that are described in the indictment and the central role that Mr. Krajisnik had in the commission of them, it's important to understand the major political events that led to the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia, and the dismemberment of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this respect, a firm understanding of the Serbian Democratic Party, Mr. Krajisnik's role in it, the evolution of the SDS party into a Bosnian Serb government, the nature of the Bosnian Serb governmental structures, and the leadership's philosophy, goals, and objectives are essential in order for you to understand this case. In my opening remarks, I will touch upon the ethnocentric political policies and strategic objectives of the SDS and the Bosnian Serb entity. These policies and objectives, which Krajisnik was instrumental in creating and implementing, were directed against non-Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina and realised on the ground through the blunt instruments of force. They tragically shaped the lives and the destinies of hundreds of thousands of people in Bosnia and have brought us together in this courtroom today. By now the history of the former Yugoslavia is well known, but it was in that milieu that the indictment was spawned, and I will therefore review with you briefly the principal political events that will figure so prominently in this case. Yugoslavia was a federal state composed of six republics and two autonomous regions, and if you, on your monitor, by pushing the -- I'm told the "computer evidence" button, there will appear before you an image showing those republics. Does the Defence have ...? All right. In the aftermath of Marshal Tito's death and the subsequent disintegration of the League of Communists, the status of these republics and the continued existence of the federation represented the major issue confronting Yugoslavia. In particular, the republics of Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, there existed dynamic and powerful but opposing socio-political forces that competed to achieve political solutions to this problem, solutions that would result either in the republics remaining within a federal structure or the republics separating from the existing federal state composition and becoming independent. In anticipation of the first multi-party elections in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were scheduled for the 18th of November, 1990, three nationalist parties emerged to challenge the entrenched communist party structure or its successors. These parties were: The Serbian Democratic Party, or SDS, which I've already mentioned, that was the party of the Bosnian Serbs; the Party of Democratic Action, or the SDA, which became the party of the Bosnian Muslims; and the Croatian Democratic Party, or HDZ, which was the party of the Bosnian Croats. The SDS party was founded on the 12th of July, 1990, and Radovan Karadzic was elected the president of the party. Mr. Krajisnik would later occupy positions on the SDS's Main Board and personnel commission. Beyond the authority reflected in these and in other positions which he held, which I will discuss shortly, the accused and Radovan Karadzic were the paramount leaders of the party. As the Chamber will learn from the evidence, they together forged policies and directives. In that effort, they were guided by Slobodan Milosevic, on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whose counsel they relied and from whose authority they drew further stature. Within Bosnia, however, it was the accused and Karadzic who together framed the policies, insisted on discipline and prodded the SDS towards a forcible separation of the mixed ethnic populations of Bosnia. In his opening speech at the SDS founding assembly, Karadzic decried what he saw as the unfavourable political position of the Serbian nation and recalled the genocide to which the Serbs had been subjected during the Second World War, a theme that would be repeated over time by Mr. Krajisnik and other SDS leaders. By inflaming the fears and passions of the Serbian population and making them susceptible to the fearsome shadows of the past, they incited the people to sever violently the bonds of peaceful co-existence that had existed between the diverse communities of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to implement the policy of ethnic cleansing. From its inception, the party's stated intention to protect the national interests of the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina included an insistence on maintaining the federal character of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the unity of all Serbs in a common state. That was their vision. Even before the first concrete steps were taken toward ethnic separation of Bosnia, the SDS warned of its categorical opposition to any effort to separate the Serbs of Bosnia from their mother country, Serbia. Let me return once again to the multi-party elections which I mentioned moments ago. In pursuit of their shared goal of defeating the Communist Party and its successors, the three parties - the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ - arrived at informal agreements to refrain from attacking one another and to cooperate in the division of power if they prevailed in the election. These agreements, while temporarily expedient, ignored their conflicting visions for the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, could you please bear in mind that you are being interpreted into two languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will slow down. The results of the election were stunning. As the nationalist parties defeated their opponents, winning electoral margins roughly proportional to their numbers in the population itself. The SDA, the Muslim party, won 86 of the total 240 seats in the assembly. The SDS, the Serbs, won 72 seats, and the HDZ, the party of the Croats, won 44 seats. Eight remaining parties shared the remaining 38 seats. The nationalist parties then faithfully implemented their interparty agreements and the SDA party of the Bosnian Muslims designated the late Alija Izetbegovic to be president of the presidency; the SDS, the party of the Bosnian Serbs, elected the accused, Momcilo Krajisnik, to be president of the Assembly; and Jure Pelivan was named by the HDZ party, the party of the Croats, to be the prime minister. Now, the SDS electoral success gave rise to another powerful party organ. In this newly elected assembly, the Serbian delegates formed the Serbian Deputies Club, a caucus created to debate and formulate SDS policies and positions to be taken in the assembly. It was this body that would eventually transform itself into the first parallel Serbian government organ, the Assembly of the Serbian People, with the accused as its president. Although the parties found common ground in their electoral campaign, they did not ever reach a common position on the most crucial issue that would face Bosnia and Herzegovina, its status in a disintegrating Yugoslavia, and this failure would prove to be both highly divisive and later fatal. In other republics of Yugoslavia, dramatic events occurred that were to plant the seed of conflict in the bosom of Bosnia. On the 25th of June, 1991, the republics of Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. The next day, the JNA engaged in armed conflict in Slovenia, and later, fighting erupted and intensified in Croatia. The possibility that the contagion of independence would spread to Bosnia greatly alarmed Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and other members of the SDS leadership, and it was anathema to them. Radovan Karadzic, speaking on behalf of the SDS leadership, repeatedly stated, and I will use his words: "The SDS will not accept an independent Croatia, or an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina." He declared again and again that the SDS would not accept any situation in which the Bosnian Serbs were not part of a common state with other Serbs in Yugoslavia. I will quote Mr. Karadzic again: "We are now openly saying what we could not -- what could not even be whispered before. The Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina pin all their hopes on their mother country, Serbia, and will never allow a state border to separate them from Serbia." The Bosnian Serbs sought to preserve their union with Yugoslavia through negotiations with the other political parties, while at the same time taking parallel steps toward ethnic separation, beginning with the creation of Serb communities of municipalities. I'll discuss Serb communities and municipalities in greater detail later in my remarks. They also sought to achieve their objectives in various international negotiations as well, which I will not describe in detail in these remarks, but those negotiations also failed. For example, on the 27th of August, 1991, the European Community established a conference on Yugoslavia that held multiple sessions in the Hague, through the 14th of August, 1992. These talks were under the chairmanship of Lord Carrington, a former British foreign minister, Cyrus Vance, a former United States department of state, Secretary of State, acted as the personal representative of the UN Secretary-General in these discussions. In its approach to Bosnia and Herzegovina, the European Community sought territorial division that would create three largely autonomous entities while normally preserving a central Bosnia and Herzegovina state. These notions were incorporated into a statement of principles agreed on the 23rd of February, 1992, which read in part that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be a state composed of three constituent units, based on national principles and taking into account ethnic, economic - I'm sorry - taking into account economic, geographic, and other criteria. In fact each constituent unit was to be dominated by a single group, Serb, Croat, or Muslim. Following the acceptance of these principles in Lisbon, the Bosnian Serb leadership returned to Sarajevo. They were elated. However, Alija Izetbegovic backed away from this agreement. At the time the Bosnian Serbs were engaged in negotiations to achieve their objectives, Radovan Karadzic made clear to the SDS that it would use force and was prepared to use force if necessary to ensure that the Bosnian Serbs were not separated from Serbia. He warned that if Bosnia was declared sovereign and independent, then "all conditions for civil war would be in place." The SDS leadership was supported in this position by Slobodan Milosevic, the president of Serb. Milosevic unequivocally insisted that Serbs remain in one state, and he said, and I quote him: "As far as the Serbian people are concerned, they want to live in one state. Hence division into several states, which would separate Serbian people and force them to live in separate sovereign states, is, from our point of view, unacceptable. That is, let me specify: Out of the question." Our evidence will show that the SDS leadership, including Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and others, collaborated closely with Milosevic and existing federal structures, such as the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, and the federal police, as it prepared and eventually implemented the forcible division of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the removal of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the territories claimed by the Serbs. As I said earlier, while the Bosnian Serb leaders were seeking to achieve their objectives through negotiations they began to prepare and organise for the creation of separate Serbian territory in Bosnia. They began that process by creating regional structures in autonomous regions, their unstated purpose being to delineate so-called Serbian territories and to establish control over large portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Bosnian Serb leaders also arranged, through the assistance of the federal authorities, to arm the Bosnian Serb population. They created secret communication systems and they issued organisational instructions for the takeover of power at the municipal level. Now, let me start with regionalisation. Faced with the possibility of Bosnian independence, the SDS began the process of separating territories. This process essentially mimicked events that occurred in Croatia, where, in 1990, Croatian Serbs had declared communities of municipalities which they then transformed into autonomous regions. The SDS in Bosnia initiated a similar process. In April of 1991, when the founding assembly of the community of municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina was held, the SDS claimed that this community of municipalities was simply an economic and developmental link of the type permitted under the Bosnian constitution, but other parties quickly denounced the community of municipalities as a transparent step towards the creation of Serbian-controlled territories. Those concerns were realised in the economic pretext exposed in September of 1991, when the community of municipalities transformed itself into the Autonomous Region of Krajina, or, as I will be referring to it throughout the remainder of my remarks, the ARK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, it's not until this moment that the French translation was able to translate your words, so if you would take a bit more breath now and then, that will allow the translators to take some breath at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I apologise to the translators. They do excellent work, and I'm sorry to put them through such a difficult pace. I will continue and I will try to slow down. The ARK regional staff, and later War Presidency, was the largest and most active of the Serb autonomous regions. The ARK Crisis Staff was instrumental in the implementation and advancement of SDS policies in the Bosnian Krajina region. Its activities included communicating republican-level SDS instructions to municipal Crisis Staff, covertly supplying weapons to Serbs, ordering the termination of non-Serbs from their jobs, and close coordination with Bosnian Serb forces in the Krajina. The ARK Crisis Staff and the ARK War Presidency were both headed by Radoslav Brdjanin, who is specifically identified in the indictment as being a member of the joint criminal enterprise. Now, at the same time, other autonomous regions were declared, encompassing large portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And again, Your Honours, I direct your attention to the monitor, and I can explain what this image depicts. This image depicts the various autonomous regions. The ARK Serb Autonomous Region, the Krajina is in blue, and in that ARK region you'll see a number of municipalities from the indictment itself. Then the additional autonomous regions are: One in pink, which is the Northern Bosnian Autonomous Region; one in peach, Semberija; one in green, Romanija-Birac autonomous region; and finally in yellow, Herzegovina autonomous region. The autonomous regions established governmental structures and were shortly afterward proclaimed as part of the territory embraced by the self-declared Serbian Republic. Once the autonomous regions had served their purpose, and once approximately 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been forcibly seized by the Bosnian Serb forces, the Bosnian Serb leadership disbanded the autonomous regions. As Karadzic would later tell the Bosnian Serb Assembly, once they had served their purpose, they were ended. Before that, however, they had proven an effective vehicle for the dismemberment of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the attainment of control over large swathes of Bosnian territory on which hundreds of thousands of Muslims had lived until 1992. Now, another manner in which the Bosnian Serbs began to organise and prepare, and which, in particular, the way the SDS began to organise for the creation and separation of the territory, was to provide arms to the Serb population. In 1991, Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership were concerned. The Serbs did not have enough arms. I would like to play for you an intercepted conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik from the 23rd of September, in which the topic of arms is discussed with them, and in which they expressed their concern that the Serbs do not have enough arms. So if we could begin that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Is it Delimustafic? Radovan KARADZIC: No, no it's Izetbegovic. Izetbegovic passed a decision at the Presidency that each station be formed according to its own need, that is, to increase the numbers of the reserve force. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah. Radovan KARADZIC: Therefore, we would have to inform our people in the Krajina and in the eastern ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, yes, you know what I'd like to ask you... We could reach an agreement with regard to that. Everything has its, you know, black and white version always. And a smart man always uses what he finds suitable for him. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I would not prevent anything. On the contrary, I'd say, "all right, all right, but there's you know... Everything has it's..." Radovan KARADZIC: Well, all right. In Serbs areas they don't have enough weapons, they don't have enough weapons. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right, but we're analysing, Radovan, please. Let me tell me something, I would like to ask you something in connection to that. We should weigh things well. What you said last night was smart. We must always see what the means. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I know what it is. As soon as we know what someone wants... Radovan KARADZIC: Look, there's a man from the police sitting with me here who understands the situation. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: Ah, Plavsic right. Just a moment. On which one? All right. All right. I'll call you in a minute. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: I'm waiting for a journalist here. Can you pop down here for a while so we can sit down? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Where are you now? Radovan KARADZIC: At the party. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: When would you come? Radovan KARADZIC: In about 15, 20 minutes. Can you make it? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Can I come at about, say, a quarter to 3.00? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes, you can. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. I'll come at a quarter to 3.00. Radovan KARADZIC: Right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the tape they're speaking even quicker, so if you'd like a little break after having heard the tape. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How is it possible that the arming process was achieved? It was achieved through the cooperation and the assistance of the Yugoslavian federal authorities whose leadership shared the goals and objectives of the Bosnian Serbs. We intend to lead considerable evidence about the arming effort, but let me provide you with some examples of that evidence now. We will tender a 20 March 1992 report of JNA General Milutin Kukanjac, drafted to the JNA General Staff, in which he reports having distributed to "volunteer units" 51.900 weapons. And reports that the SDS had distributed 17.298 weapons to such volunteer units. Now, these were -- these volunteer units were not part of the composition of the JNA. You will also hear specific evidence about a meeting that took place in April of 1991 in Belgrade in the office of Mihalj Kertes, the assistant to the minister of the interior, over one year prior to the takeover of the Bratunac and Srebrenica municipalities. The participants in that meeting were Miroslav Deronjic, a leading SDS political figure in the Bratunac municipality, and Goran Zekic, who was the representative from Srebrenica to the Bosnian Serb Assembly. At that meeting, arrangements were made to provide arms to the Bosnian Serbs of the Bratunac and Srebrenica municipalities in Eastern Bosnia. Mihalj Kertes, as our evidence will show, was in frequent contact with the Bosnian Serb leadership. During the meeting in April of 1991, he said to Messrs. Deronjic and Zekic, and I quote: "That in the area of 50 kilometres from the Drina River, everything would be fully Serb." As you will hear later in my remarks when I discuss the strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina that were announced by Radovan Karadzic at the Bosnian Serb Assembly 13 months later, Kertes's statement to Messrs. Deronjic and Zekic virtually mirrors one of the explicit strategic objectives, and I'm referring to strategic objective number 3. Now, the paramount role of the SDS in the arming activity and the symbiotic relationship that it had with Slobodan Milosevic and the federal authorities was explained in August of 1993 at the 34th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly by General Milan Gvero, the assistant commander of the VRS for morale, religious, and legal affairs. Let me quote what General Gvero told that Assembly, and I quote: "The Serbian Democratic Party, which politically awakened and homogenised the Serbian people, formulated the political and social goals in organisational terms, all the important prerequisites for a successful struggle.." He went on to say: "The Serbian Democratic Party and the established state institutions also have the most credit for the initial arming of the Serbian people with small arms which was possible thanks to the support and cooperativeness of numerous Serbs, officers in the JNA commands on the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbs in the interior ministry and other political institutions, and officers of the army from Serbia, that is to say, the SRJ, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." Now, in their preparations, the SDS also established communications network throughout the Bosnian Serb communities so that, as Karadzic later explained, and again I quote him: "Information from the most remote villages reaches the SDS Main Board in two hours at most." According to SDS operational guidelines that were issued on the 15th of August, 1991, each member of the local SDS board was required to "keep contact with 10 to 20 households." This network was not only established to relay general information but to convey orders. SDS members were obliged to carry out and respect decisions of party organs. Because this is a trial of a politician at the very apex of SDS and later Republika Srpska power, it is worth emphasising the nature of the SDS leadership's viewpoint on the adherence to and implementation of its policies. During the second session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held on the 21st of November, 1991, the accused issued a stern warning to the SDS members. Quoting his words: "We would like to send the following message to all those who falter, or are neutral, weak, or misguided, and who do not feel like traitors. Today you still have time. Tomorrow it will be too late." Three months later, at the eighth Bosnian Serb Assembly held on the 25th of February, 1992, Radovan Karadzic re-echoed the stern warning of the accused. He said that once the party adopted a policy, and I quote him: "Anything else is treason. Anything outside the adopted policy is treason. Assisting the enemy cannot be tolerated. Giving him a way out and confusing the people while being a member of that party, of the Assembly, and the party organs, that cannot be. I will not allow it. I will signal to the people: People, this man is a traitor." Such sentiments were echoed by Radoslav Brdjanin, the head of the SDS party, the head of the ARK Crisis Staff and War Presidency. Quoting

utterances.speaker: MR. BRDJANIN
utterances.text: "I am a man who abides by two principles. I obey and respect those who are above me, all those who are under my command must obey me." The evidence will show that as the SDS moved closer to the implementation of a policy of forcible division in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was heightened need for constant information that could be securely and secretly transmitted. The SDS created a security system whose organisation and functioning was to be strictly conspiratorial and organised on a hierarchical principle. This security system created codes for communication via public phones, secret designations were established for other SDS municipal boards, and the SDS established a 24-hour, seven-day-a-week watch service at party headquarters. Let me again return to the words of General Gvero from the 34th Bosnian Serb assembly session: "The SDS formulated the political and social goals and prepared in organisational terms all the important prerequisites for a successful struggle." At the time the SDS was clandestinely preparing for the possible separation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and negotiating internationally in an effort to separate Bosnia by agreement, the Serbian position in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly became hard and menacing. At that session, at a session of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly held on the 14th of October, 1991, and presided over by Mr. Krajisnik in his capacity as president of that Assembly, the Assembly considered a platform on the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the future structure of the Yugoslav community and a memorandum letter of intentions. These documents together stated that Bosnia and Herzegovina would participate in the future Yugoslav state only to the same extent that Croatia and Slovenia participated. You'll recall that they had declared their independence. Radovan Karadzic took the floor and warned in unequivocal terms what would happen to the Muslims if they persisted in pursuing independence. He said they might disappear because they could not defend themselves. Let us listen to a portion of that speech. Again, if you turn to your monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRDJANIN
utterances.text: "Radovan KARADZIC: We have the constitution that will prevent you from voting. Even if you brought a decision today that would be a shame for Izetbegovic in The Hague because we do have a way in The Hague."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Lest there be any doubt what Karadzic meant by the word "disappear" in his speech, our evidence will include an intercepted telephone conversation between Karadzic and Gojko Dogo, the president of the Association of Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina. This conversation was intercepted two days prior to the speech that you just heard. In that conversation, Karadzic explains that, at best, the Muslims could hope for some enclaves in Bosnia in which most of the territory would be Serb and which would be a unit in a federation of the rump Yugoslavia. As he said: "We could accept them creating, let's call it, a Muslim district in their area within Yugoslavia." He went on to say "or several enclaves." He goes on to say in that intercepted conversation that should the Muslims persist in their demands, and I quote this intercept: "They will disappear. That people will disappear from the face of the earth if they start now. Our offer was their only chance." He goes on: "They don't understand that here there will be blood to the knees and that the Muslim people will disappear." Now, throughout this conversation, his grim prophecy is repeated. I'm going to quote him again: "They have to know that there are 20.000 armed Serbs around Sarajevo. They will -- they will disappear. Sarajevo will be a black cauldron where 300.000 Muslims will die. They're not right in the head. I don't know. Now I will have to talk to them openly. 'People, don't screw around. There are three, four hundred thousand armed Serbs in Bosnia. What are you thinking of? Plus there's an army and the hardware and everything. Do you think you can secede like Croatia?'" Later on in that same intercepted conversation, he says: "They don't understand that. They will be up to their necks in blood and that the Muslim people will disappear. The poor Muslims would disappear who don't know where he is taking them, where he is taking the Muslims." And I'll cite one more passage from that intercepted conversation, this is Karadzic again: "They simply don't have any way to carry out a secession. I think that this is clear to the army and clear to everyone. It will be a real bloodbath. This time the army won't only use two planes any more of the 500 it has; it will use 20 for each assault." At this same session, where Karadzic gave this chilling speech, Mr. Krajisnik, the speaker of the Assembly, closed the session in order to prevent a vote from being taken on the memorandum and platform. Serb deputies walked out. But before the closing of the session, Mr. Krajisnik warned the non-Serb deputies, and I'll use his words: "I just want to tell you: Think carefully about what will happen to you if you try to adopt anything outside this assembly. I will not warn you individually. You know that very well." And then he concluded his remarks and the assembly closed. However, Mr. Krajisnik's parliamentary manoeuvre failed. Following the walkout of the Bosnian Serb deputies, the vice-president of the Assembly, Mariofil Ljubic, a member of the HDZ party, reopened the session, and a vote was taken on the proposed platform and memorandum. Both items passed. In the aftermath of the passing the declaration of sovereignty, the SDS accelerated the steps to divide Bosnia. On the night of the 15th of October, the SDS political council met, attended by the entire SDS leadership, including Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Biljana Plavsic, Nikola Koljevic. As one of the attendees, Tudor Dutina, observed, and I quote: "This evening, we must shed the illusion that a form of co-existence with the Muslims and the Croats can be found." Three days later, the Serbian Deputies Club convened a session at which the Bosnian Serb leadership emphasised that the SDS was moving forward with the division of Bosnia. Karadzic announced that he would put the party in a state of emergency. On the 24th of October, 1991, the SDS delegates to the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly met separately and established the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'll refer to this later as the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Mr. Krajisnik was named the president of that most important body and declared at that session, among other things, that the Assembly had been founded with the purpose of ensuring that the Serb people would have its destiny in its own hands, and he said what that meant was that the will of the Serbian people was to remain "in its historical and ethnic territories, as part of a joint state of Yugoslavia." Karadzic also declared that this event was an historic step, and he said: "This is an historic step, a step the Serbian people takes to shatter the last illusions and to round our entity in such a way that it would never again find itself endangered from within." The same day, Karadzic told the Serbian president Milosevic what would happen if the Bosnian Serbs [sic] insisted on pursuing independence. That conversation was intercepted, and in that conversation, as you will hear in just a moment, Karadzic says that they had prepared everything, that the Bosnians would break their teeth, that there would be no way that they would live together in a country with them. So if we could now play that intercept. This is a portion of the intercept, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "Radovan KARADZIC: Hello? Slobodan MILOSEVIC: How is the work going? Radovan KARADZIC: It's coming along slowly. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Have you arranged it with Alija to abolish those decisions of his? Radovan KARADZIC: Well, we gave him until 1700 hours to abolish them but they won't. They will never manage to do it in time. They've made so many that they can't abolish them. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: All right, then. You can extend the deadline if they intend to abolish them. Radovan KARADZIC: No, they don't think that the Hague -- I mean to abolish them. They don't mean to abolish them. They think they're doing it legally but we'll respond with all means possible. We will establish Yugoslavia and all the areas where we live. We have a constitution. If they abolish their BiH constitution we'll rely on this which is older, and I mean the federal constitution. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes, yes, but they're not foolish enough to continue in that direction. Radovan KARADZIC: No, they want The Hague, that is, Europe, to give them a state in which we would be locked by international agreements. We can't allow that. We have to prepare everything and we have prepared everything to create a de facto situation that cannot be challenged which they will break their teeth on. They simply have to break them. There's no way we will live in a country with them. No. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Why don't you, I mean, have a talk with Alija and tell him exactly that. Radovan KARADZIC: Alija is focussed on his goal with the conviction of a religious fanatic and he cannot be talked to. I would like to talk to him, but that we don't touch anything of his. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes, yes, but why don't you tell him exactly that, explain to him and put it to him nicely and then say please go ahead, abolish it. Radovan KARADZIC: No, no, believe me, there is no chance of that. He would just waste our time. He wasted three months on the cantonisation of Bosnia and then he showed up with just a ... With a paper that Tudjman gave him. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Very well, then. All right."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You will hear that intercept in the course of this trial, but in addition, Mr. Karadzic said that it was the intention of the Bosnian Serbs to establish full authority over Serbian territories in Bosnia, and he went on to say that Izetbegovic "will not have control over 65 per cent of his territory. That is our goal." Now, among the decisions taken by the newly founded Serbian Assembly, Bosnian Serbian Assembly, I'm sorry, was the decision to hold a plebiscite on the 9th and 10th of November. And the question to be put to the Serbian people was: "Do you agree with the decision that the Serbian people shall stay in the joint state of Yugoslavia together with," and it identifies other entities. The Assembly of the Bosnian Serb People also declared, and I quote relevant parts of this declaration: "That there is a conspiracy underway that started a long time ago, and it is aimed at reducing the Serbian people, a constituentive people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, into a national minority. Because of the tragic events that the Serbian people had experienced this century, particularly the genocide it was exposed to, it taught the Serbian people a lesson, and we have established an assembly." He went on to say and to suggest that similar events were looming over the destiny of the Serb people and that the Serb people had a right, an intrinsic right, to form their own state. On the 9th and 10th a plebiscite was indeed held. The Serbs who voted in it rejected independence and elected to stay in association -- remain in the state of Yugoslavia. The Bosnian Serb leadership would repeatedly invoke the plebiscite to legitimacise [sic] further steps toward ethnic separation. Your Honour, I'm unsure when we are planning to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just thinking about having one break, but then little bit longer. I know that the tapes last for a little bit over one and a half hours. So if you could continue for another 15 to 20 minutes, we would then have a bit of a longer break and then continue until 7.00, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I was discussing the clandestine efforts of the SDS to take control in Bosnia, and these efforts took other forms as well. On the 19th of December, 1991, Bosnian Serb municipal leaders were summoned to Sarajevo, where they received strictly confidential written instructions outlining steps for the takeover of power at the grass-roots level. The instructions which we will introduce into evidence in the course of the trial, are entitled "Instructions for the organisation and activity of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in extraordinary circumstances." They were prepared and issued by the SDS Main Board, of which the accused was a prominent member. They applied to municipalities where Serbs were a minority of the population and where they were a majority, and they were clear and simple instructions. In municipalities where the Serbs were a majority of the population, variant A, and in municipalities where the Serbs were in a minority of the population, variant B, a Serbian Municipal Assembly was to be formed, and preparations were to be undertaken for the establishment of other municipal organs. These included preparations for taking over police personnel, and facilities. In both variant A and B municipalities, a crisis staff of the Serbian people was to be formed which was to be responsible for activating police, Territorial Defence, and civilian defence formations, as well as a variety of other defence-related tasks. For both variant A and variant B municipalities, the instructions were broken down into two phases. In phase one, SDS leaders were instructed to form crisis staffs, proclaim Serbian assemblies, and prepare for the formation of municipal government bodies. In the second phase, SDS leaders were to establish the new municipal organs, mobilise Serb members of the police, ensure a call-up of JNA reserves and Territorial Defence units, and take other steps in preparation for conflict. This second phase was to be initiated by the SDS president, using a secret, pre-established procedure. During the course of this trial, we will present evidence to you how those instructions were implemented in various municipalities. Now, returning to the next significant event, on the 17th of December, 1991, European Community ministers approved a procedure for Yugoslavia's republics to apply for independence and created a commission, later known as the Badinter Commission, to assess such applications. Three days later, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina presidency voted to apply to the Badinter Commission for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be recognised as an independent state. Now, the very next day, the Bosnian Serb Assembly convened, presided over by the accused, and it took various decisions, including a decision to initiate the establishment of the Republika Srpska, and it recognised the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The Assembly also issued a warning to the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which stated that it would never accept, under any circumstances, to be subordinated to anybody, and especially not to accept the status of a minority. During this session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, one of the Bosnian Serb representatives, Radoslav Vukic, the head of the Banja Luka SDS municipal board and member of the Main and Executive Boards, stated, to applause, and I quote: "If the European Community goes on with its threat to recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state, or as a part of a future independent state of Croatia, or the independent state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there will be another Serbian uprising and there will be massive bloodshed, in which some nations that have been subsequently created will disappear altogether." Karadzic then gave a lengthy speech, and I quote from parts of it: "We have the right and the ability to prevent anybody on the territories where we conducted our referendum to secede from Yugoslavia. In all territories where Serbs took part in the referendum, regardless of whether they make up 5 per cent or 55 per cent of the population, they are the constituent element of that town or that republic. All territories where we voted in our referendum to remain within Yugoslavia must stay within Yugoslavia if we so decide." He went on to say: "We can accommodate everything. Everything is better than civil war. Everything is better than imposing one's solutions on to others. Everything is better than chaos and hell, which we can see developing and evolving. We are committed not to instigate any such thing. Even more, we are committed not to take part in any such thing, unless it is imposed upon us in a way that it was imposed on our brothers in Croatia." In that speech, he goes on to say: "Apart from causing the deaths of several hundred thousand people and complete destruction of several hundred towns, a civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina would also result in massive and rapid population movements, in other words, it would lead to population homogenisation. What would be the end of it all? The end result would be as it is today, separate Serbian, Croatian, and Muslim areas, left impoverished by several hundred towns and several hundred thousand people." Finally, he says: "It seems to me that at this moment in time, and the amount of mutual suspicion, we should aim for as much separation as possible, and only later let life and economic reasons bring the people together. We should not aim to separate 30 per cent now and leave 70 per cent, as it is because the tensions that exist between us will not be resolved. Everything that can exist independently should be separated." On the 9th of January, 1992, the Bosnian Serb Assembly proclaimed the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This included, and I quote: "Areas where the Serbian people are a minority because of the genocide conducted against it in the Second World War." On the 15th of January, 1992, the Badinter Commission reported its recommendation that Bosnia and Herzegovina be required to hold a referendum to determine the will of its people regarding independence. On the 24th and 25th of January, in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly, the delegates considered a resolution to hold such a referendum on the 29th of February to the 1st of March, 1992. The Serb delegates strenuously objected and the accused tried to close the session. The SDS delegates walked out, and thereafter, a vote on whether to hold the referendum was held, and it passed. The next day, the Bosnian Serb Assembly announced that this decision was illegal. Shortly thereafter, on the 14th of February, 1992, Karadzic ordered the activation of the second phase of the variant A and B instructions at an expanded deputies club session. As Karadzic told the media the next day, and I quote: "The Serbs have created a comprehensive programme for full control of the territory where they are an ethnic majority." On the 28th of February, 1992, the Bosnian Serb Assembly adopted the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was later to be promulgated. On that date, the Bosnian Serb Assembly passed, and the accused signed, significant legislation directing that Bosnia and Herzegovina police stations on Serb-claimed territory would cease to function as of the 1st of April, 1992 and would be replaced by police units of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 27th of March, 1992, the Bosnian Serb Assembly promulgated the constitution that was previously adopted. It also created a government. It elected a prime minister and created a national security council which acted as a de facto presidency. Momcilo Krajisnik was a member of the national security council. On the 31st of March, 1992, the order calling for the separation of the police forces was sent out and non-Serbs who refused to wear new Serb insignia and swear loyalty to the Bosnian Serb authorities were dismissed from their police jobs. Your Honour, I think this might be an appropriate place for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon, although it's a bit -- I'll ask the registrar: How -- and may I also ask the interpreters whether one break would do if we would then continue until 7.00, at what time could we restart? Because it's hardly of any use to have two breaks, I would say. Would a break until a quarter past 5.00 be sufficient? And may I ask you, Mr. Harmon, how much time you'd still need, approximately, to finish your opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, given how slowly I am required to speak, Your Honour, it's difficult to make that projection. I hope and will endeavour to finish by 7.00, but I'm not entirely confident I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at both technicians and interpreters, a restart at a quarter past 5.00, would that be possible, and can we continue up until 7.00, or would that be too long? The problem always is to hear from the booth. If I'm on one channel I would not hear the other booth. Could perhaps the English booth give me the information needed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, since the English booth is not really working, it's up to the B/C/S and the French booth to decide if it's okay to work from 5.15 until 7.00. So we leave it up to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, if the other booth would tell us what would be the maximum time they could continue if we would ... Thank you very much. I heard from the French booth that we could continue at a quarter past 5.00 and then continue until 7.00. We are adjourned until a quarter past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I ended with the end of a long description on the political events that set the stage for what now happens in these crimes -- in this indictment, which is the crimes themselves. So we ended on the events of the 31st of March, 1992, when the separation of the police forces in Bosnia took place. Now, as the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina became imminent, Bosnian Serb forces, in conjunction with the JNA, Serbian police, and Bosnian and Serbian paramilitaries started violently seizing territory that would comprise the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and ethnically cleansing the non-Serbs from that territory, territory in which they had lived for generations. Our evidence will show that these violent events started in the municipality of Bijeljina on the 31st of March, 1992. There, paramilitary forces of the notorious paramilitary leader Arkan were particularly brutal in their attacks on the civilian population. They terrorised the civilian population, and those civilians bore the brunt of this savagery. I would like to have the next exhibit displayed. This image, which shocked the world, is a piece of evidence that we will present during the course of this trial. It is an image that was taken in Bijeljina, on or about the 31st of March, when Arkan's troops seized the municipality, along with other Bosnian Serb forces. This image depicts representatives, members of the Arkan paramilitary group. Let me tell you a little bit about Arkan and what our evidence will show. I've lost my image here. Could I have the image back, please? Let me tell you a little bit about Arkan, who had earned a reputation and a widespread reputation for his brutal efforts against the Croats in Croatia. He was embraced during this time period by Biljana Plavsic, a leading Bosnian Serb figure who is identified as a member of the joint criminal enterprise. We will now play a very brief clip, and before we play it, let me describe what it is for Your Honours. This is a video clip of Mrs. Plavsic greeting Arkan in Bijeljina during that period of time. It's a very quick clip. It will be played twice. And if we could proceed with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's no reason to translate. Could you stop it right there, please? Pause. Mrs. Plavsic, a member of the joint criminal enterprise, is the female who is between the two men whose backs are facing you, and the paramilitary leader, Arkan, is the gentleman she is kissing. So if we could now continue with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm told that's the end of the movie. We now have -- okay. Then that concludes with that particular image. Eight months after the events in Bijeljina, at the 22nd session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, Mrs. Plavsic revealed her role in bringing Arkan to Bijeljina. I quote her: "After the statement of the president of the Republic, that is, after the call to all volunteers in Serbian countries and in all Orthodox countries, I have sent a letter to all addresses. I will tell you: I was trying to get together all people willing to fight for the Serbian cause, and then letters were sent. You talk about paramilitary units and about paramilitary units. Pardon me, it doesn't concern me. I was asking for men willing to fight for the Serbian cause, men willing to fight on the territory of the Republika Srpska. These letters were sent to the Soviet Union, they were sent to Seselj, to Arkan, to Jovic." As an intercepted telephone communication that we will present in the course of this trial reveals, she later invited Arkan to come to Sarajevo. Now, the evidence will show that the savage events that occurred in Bijeljina were repeated time and time again by Bosnian Serb and Serbian forces, including paramilitary formations, in municipality after municipality. In those municipalities, the permanent removal of Bosnian Muslim, Bosnian Croat, and other non-Serbs was affected by murder, unlawful detention, forcible transfer or deportation of non-Serbs. During this trial, you will hear considerable evidence from the victims of these crimes, and I will not detail that evidence now. Our evidence will demonstrate beyond any doubt that the events in those municipalities were not spontaneous or random events but were the results of policies conceived of by the accused and other members of the criminal enterprise, and implemented by forces under his control. Now, on the 6th of April, the European Community recognised Bosnia as an independent and sovereign state, and on that same day, the Bosnian Serb Assembly declared the independence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would like to fast-forward to the 12th of May, five weeks after this independence was declared, and I'm referring to the 12th of May, 1992, to the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, presided over by the accused. This was a very important Assembly session, because at that session, the Bosnian Serb army was established, Ratko Mladic was selected as the commander of the main staff of that army, and, as you know, General Mladic is identified in the indictment as a member of the joint criminal enterprise. Our evidence will show that Ratko Mladic was personally selected to lead the new Bosnian Serb army by the accused and by Karadzic. In a speech at the 50th Bosnian Serb Assembly, Radovan Karadzic explained how he and the accused made their choice, and I quote: "Gentlemen, we got the officers we asked for. I asked for Mladic. General Ninkovic, then a colonel, and General Perisic, had visited me before that, and I had noticed Mladic's blunt statements in the newspapers. He was already in Knin then. I took an interest in him, and together with Mr. Krajisnik, I went to General Kukanjac's office and listened to him issuing orders and commanding around Kupres and Knin. We spent countless nights in the office of General Kukanjac at that time. President Krajisnik was already the president of the Assembly, and I was just the president of the party. I did not have any state function. We asked for Mladic and said that they should set up the headquarters as they saw fit. We wouldn't interfere." Now, two weeks before the VRS was formally established at the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the accused participated in another high-level meeting, this time with Milosevic, Karadzic, and members of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia presidency, Branko Kostic, Momir Bulatovic, and Borisav Jovic. The topic under discussion at that meeting was the transformation of the JNA in Bosnia into the Army of the Republika Srpska. According to the diary of Borisav Jovic, who was a member of the SFRY presidency, let me quote this entry: "The Security Council has recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina. Interethnic fighting has broken out there. It is being demanded that we withdraw the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Slobodan and I both expected and predicted this. There remain around 90.000 JNA soldiers in that Republic, mostly of Serb nationality, over whom the Serb leadership from Bosnia and Herzegovina can assume political command. Karadzic agrees. Krajisnik raises a series of questions: How will that military be financed? Who will pay its wages? Who will provide its pensions? Et cetera. All of which are indeed problems but are not critical to our discussion. There was plenty back and forth about the deadline for withdrawal, and in the end, we agreed to complete it within 15 days. Since it is also necessary to withdraw generals who are not originally from Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was agreed that General Mladic would replace General Vukovic. For us, this action was very significant, but for the Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was even more significant. They got their own military." Now, I said this particular session of the Assembly was very important. There were other important decisions taken at that Assembly. The presidency of the Serb Republic was also established, replacing the acting presidency of Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic. The presidency then consisted of Karadzic, Plavsic, and Koljevic. In addition, the presidency was designated as the supreme commander of the armed forces. Now, let me digress here for just a moment, because I've been using terms like "expanded presidency," "acting presidency," and it's very, very confusing. So let me try to clarify that, in your minds, and I will do so or attempt to do so by using this next exhibit, which if it could be put on the screen. And I don't see it on my screen, Ms. Javier. There it is. You'll see in this chart the various iterations of the presidency of the Republika Srpska in 1992. You will see on the 28th of February, the acting presidency that consisted of two individuals: Nikola Koljevic, now deceased, Biljana Plavsic, identified as a member of the joint criminal enterprise. That was replaced on the 12th of May by a three-member presidency: Radovan Karadzic, Nikola Koljevic, and Biljana Plavsic. On the 2nd of June, 1992, there was an expanded presidency. This consisted of five people. And you will see that one of those members of the expanded presidency is the accused. That expanded presidency lasted from June 2nd, 1992 until the 17th of December, 1992. And finally, the presidency, with a president, Radovan Karadzic, was established on the 17th of December, 1992, and there were two vice-presidents. Returning again to this very important Assembly session. At this session on the 12th of May, Karadzic announced the six strategic objectives of the Serbian people which had been formulated by the senior Bosnian Serb leadership, including the accused. These strategic objectives are quite important. They were the official expression of policy developed, shaped, and promoted by the accused, and their revelation to the Assembly on the 12th of May was not an epiphany. They clearly had been known and understood by their Serb audience and they were the culmination of the previous discussions amongst the leading members of the SDS and their allies in Serbia. Indeed, let me focus your attention on what Karadzic said about two months earlier at the 11th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. He said, and I quote: "You all know our strategic plans. The ultimate strategic goal must remain secret." Now, Your Honours, let me have the next exhibit, please. What were these strategic objectives? I have now had them placed before Your Honours on the screen, and you can see these objectives were promulgated on the 12th of May, signed by the president of the National Assembly, the accused. And these objectives are as follows: 1. Establish state borders separating Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities. 2. Set up a corridor between Semberija and Krajina. 3. Establish a corridor in the Drina River Valley, that is, eliminate the Drina as a border separating Serb states. 4. Establish a border on the Una and Neretva Rivers. 5. Divide the city of Sarajevo into Muslim parts, Serbian parts, and establish effective state authorities in both parts. 6. Ensure the access to the sea for the Republika Srpska. Now, at that Assembly session, what did Karadzic have to say about each of these objectives? I quote him: "The first goal is the separation from the two national communities, separation of states." Now, before explaining this objective, let's examine a map. And if I could have the next exhibit placed on the computer screen. This is a map, Your Honours, showing both Croatia and Bosnia. It is a map showing the distribution of Serbs and the concentration of the Serb populations in those two states. The legend shows you that those areas in white have the fewest number of Serbs; the areas in the darkest blue have the most. Now, if you notice, there is a dark line on the map, starting at the bottom, running at about a 45-degree angle. Ms. Javier is pointing that out. That is the border between Croatia and Bosnia. And you will see in this map a considerable mixing of the populations. There are some areas where it's dark blue and some areas where there's no blue. Now, after examining this map, let's listen to what Mr. Karadzic had to say when he defined the separation of states. He said: "Separation from those who are our enemies, who have used every opportunity, especially this century, to attack us, and who would continue such practices if we were to stay together in the same state." Now, the meaning of this objective was understood by everyone who was in attendance at the Assembly session. It was an often repeated tenet of the leadership's philosophy. Indeed, earlier, at an SDS Deputies' Club session on the 28th of February, 1992, which was attended by the accused, this is what Karadzic had to say, and I quote: "It is our goal for Croatia to consolidate its territory, but it is clear to every Serb that Croats and Serbs cannot live in a single state." He then went on to say: "The conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina is basically a conflict among peoples. Just as was the case between India and Pakistan, and nothing new, it resulted in a huge resettlement of people. Muslims cannot live with others. We must be clear on that. They couldn't live with the Hindu, who are as peaceful as sheep. They couldn't live with the Greek on Cyprus. They couldn't live in Lebanon with Arabs of the same blood, language, but of a different faith. There can be no discussions here. Yet they have set up the Bosnian Krajina there, and in two years' time you have problems again, to separate each and every village there, because they will overwhelm you with their birthrate and their tricks. We cannot allow that to happen." Now, I'll discuss this particular goal in greater detail in a few moments, but it's important to note that by the 12th of May, when this objective was formerly announced in the Bosnian Serb Assembly, it had already been ruthlessly implemented in municipalities such as Bijeljina, which I discussed a few minutes ago, it had been ruthlessly implemented, as our evidence will show, in Brcko, in Bosanski Novi, in the municipality of Foca, and in the municipality of Zvornik, among others. Now, the second strategic goal -- and if we could have the image on the screen, I will read what Mr. Karadzic had to say about the second strategic goal, and you'll see on this image that's before you, in the middle of the picture it says corridor objective 2. Let me read what Mr. Karadzic meant by the second strategic goal. He said that it was a corridor between Semberija and Krajina. He went on to say: "This is of the utmost strategic importance for the Serbian people because it integrates the Serbian countries, not only of Serbian BH, of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina with Serbian Krajina, and Serbian Krajina with Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia." He further said: "That is a strategic goal which we have to achieve because Krajina, Bosnian Krajina, Serbian Krajina, or the alliance of Serbian states is infeasible if we do not secure that corridor." So again, pointing as the moving arrow on this moving arrow depicts this is the area that the strategic objective number 2 applied to. As to the third strategic goal, Karadzic said: "The third strategic goal is to establish a corridor in the Drina Valley, that is, the elimination of the Drina as a border between two worlds. We are on both sides of the Drina, and it is our strategic interest and our living space." Now, recall, Your Honours, the evidence that I described to you earlier in my remarks of a meeting that took place in April, in Belgrade, between Bosnian Serb political leaders Deronjic and Zekic, 13 months before, where Mr. Kertes from the Ministry of the Interior said that 50 miles -- 50 kilometres on the other side of the Drina would be Serb. He forecast 13 months before the strategic objective number 3. As to the fourth goal, Karadzic said: "The fourth strategic goal is the establishment of the border on the Una and Neretva Rivers." And you'll see in the upper left-hand corner of this image what that goal applied to. As to the fifth strategic goal, Karadzic said: "The fifth strategic goal is the division of the city of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim parts, and the implementation of an effective state government in each of these two parts of the constitutive state." He went on to say: "In addition, the fighting in Sarajevo keeps fighting far away from Krajina, far away from Semberija, far away from Drina, far away from all of those areas, where we could possibly have conflicts with Muslims. Because the fighting around Sarajevo will decide the destiny of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we suspected and said before that if there was a war, it would start in Sarajevo and end in Sarajevo." So you can see the strategic objective number 5 identified in the map. And finally, and quite simply, the sixth strategic objective, he said, is an exit of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the sea. In that session, when Karadzic was announcing the objectives of the Serbian people, he continued by saying: "We believe, we have faith in God, justice, and our own strength, that we shall achieve what we have planned, all the six strategic goals, of course, according to the hierarchy, and that we shall finally and definitively finish the job of the freedom struggle of the Serbian people. That job is not finished." He went on to say: "We must also put an end to the Serbian megalomania, trying to include as many of our enemies in our areas as possible, especially as much territory as possible, as many hills and brooks, regardless of whether they are fertile or not. It must be brought to a reasonable measure in order for us to be solid and compact." Later he said in that same address: "I am saying this because every day we meet our brave people who took as much as they could, which may bring us in danger of including in our state too many enemies who will work against the state. We do not want to get our state with a huge number of those who are against our state." Thereafter, after this presentation by Karadzic, the strategic objectives were adopted by the Bosnian Serb Assembly, were signed by the accused in his capacity as president of that Assembly, and were distributed to the military and to other vital organs of the Bosnian Serb Republic, and they were later published in the Official Gazette. Our evidence will show that the blunt instruments of force that were at the disposal of the Bosnian Serb leadership - the army, the police, the paramilitaries - that are responsible for the ethnic cleansing unhesitatingly adopted these objectives and instructed their subordinate units about them. And I will quote from one report that we will put into evidence in this case: "The strategic objectives of our war which were promptly defined and set before the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska, the commands and the units, served as a general guideline upon which we planned the actual operations." The report goes on to say: "The Main Staff of the army translated the set of objectives into general and individual missions of the Army of the Republika Srpska and of the individual operational and tactical formations." Now, I'd like to take you through a series of Bosnian Serb army reports to show you how quickly and how thoroughly the strategic objectives were implemented. And we will lead this evidence during the course of the trial. Nine days after Karadzic announced these strategic objectives at the Assembly session, all units of the 1st Krajina Corps were informed of the following. And when I say "the 1st Krajina Corps," I'm referring to the Bosnian Serb army unit that operated in the area of the Krajina, the ARK region. This is what all the units were informed nine days after these objectives were announced in the Assembly: "The constituent Serbian people who lived on around 65 per cent of the area and represent more than 35 per cent of the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, must struggle for complete separation from Muslim and Croatian peoples and form their own state. Only after that will they be able to decide with whom and how they will unite and associate." Nineteen days after the announcement of the strategic objectives, it was reported in a confidential 1st Krajina Corps report that was sent to the Bosnian Serb Main Staff that Muslim conscripts in the army were expressing, and I quote, "dissatisfaction with the massive destruction of their towns." And it goes on to say: "This is made worse by public statements made in the media by SDS Bosanska Krajina Autonomous Region leaders who advocate moving and expelling all Muslims and Croats from these areas." The following day, 20 days after these objectives were announced, the 1st Krajina Corps reported to the VRS Main Staff command. It discussed the movements of Muslim and Croat populations from Banja Luka region, and it said, and I quote: "Those departing will not be allowed to return." The next day, General Momir Talic, who is identified in the indictment as being a member of the joint criminal enterprise, reported to the VRS Main Staff, and I quote: "The Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village has been expelled." Lisnja village was in Prnjavor. You will hear evidence from that municipality about the operations run by General Talic. On the 14th of June, 1992, General Talic reported, and I quote: "The entire zone of responsibility is fully under control." He goes on to report: "The most difficult situation concerns the Muslim and Croat refugees in the area of autonomous region Krajina, their security and provision of food. The attempt to expel them to Central Bosnia failed because of transportation and their resistance to leaving their places of residence." Now, the AR -- the Autonomous Region Krajina, or ARK, contains a number of the municipalities that are identified in the indictment. And again, we will be presenting the testimonies of many of the victims of that ethnic cleansing to Your Honours. Now, was the goal enunciated in the first strategic objective effective? Was the separation of the non-Serb population from Serb-claimed territory effective? Startlingly so. We will present evidence, including expert testimony, that the ethnic composition of Bosnia changed from being a multi-ethnic mosaic of Serb, Muslim, and Croat areas into an ethnically segregated Bosnia, with Serbs dominating the areas they sought to conquer. The effect of the first strategic objective is graphically demonstrated by the following evidence. And let me show Your Honours, if I could have the next exhibit on the screen, what Bosnia looked like in 1991. And this map depicts the distribution of the ethnic groups -- if we could move up, I believe. Is there any more of this?
