You'll see that in blue are the Croats, in green are the Bosniaks, and the Serbs are in red, and the percentages are self-explanatory on that. And this is the ethnic composition before the war in 1991. Now, keeping this map in mind and on your screens, I would like to use data taken from Bosnian Serb documents that we will introduce into evidence in the course of this trial. These documents illustrate the demographic changes in some of the municipalities in the indictment, about which you will hear evidence. In May of 1993, the Banja Luka security services centre of the Ministry of the Interior issued a list identifying citizens who had moved out of their area of responsibility. Data from eight municipalities identified in the indictment are included in this particular report. According to the 1991 census data for this area, approximately 187.000 Muslims were in those municipalities in 1991. However, according to the internal Bosnian Serb document that we will present to Your Honours, 153.723 Muslims and 6.500 Croats had left the municipality. Another report that we will present, another state security service report from the municipality of Kljuc, a municipality listed in the indictment and about which you will hear evidence, contains the following data, and it contains data regarding the ethnic composition of the municipality at the time it was sent: 18.764 Serbs, 1.445 Muslims, 124 Croats, and 187 others. According to the 1991 census, the pre-war census, the population of Kljuc as a whole had been 50 per cent Serb, 40 per cent Muslim, and 1 per cent Croat. Another confidential Bosnian Serb report from the internal affairs, this time in Banja Luka, compared the 1991 and the 1995 populations under its control. In those 25 municipalities, the previous Muslim population had been reduced from 252.566 to just 34.525, and the number of Croats had been reduced from 96.789 to just 18.932. Of the 25 municipalities listed in this confidential internal Bosnian Serb document, 13 of the municipalities are contained in our indictment. I will just extract some of the figures from some of the municipalities for purposes of illustration. In the Prijedor municipality, the location of the notorious Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps, the numbers of Muslims was reduced from nearly 50.000 to 3.600. In the municipality of Sanski Most, the number of Muslims went from 28.285 to just 3.350. In the Kljuc municipality, the number of Muslims fell from 17.714 to just over 1.200. Now, these figures are extracted from internal Bosnian Serb documents. We will also present reports from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, UNHCR, and a report published by UNHCR in 1994 contains estimates of the remarkable declines in the Muslim and Croat populations in Northern Bosnia and in Eastern Bosnia from 1991. The UNHCR estimated that the number of Muslims (261.003) and the Croats (40.638) in Eastern Bosnia had declined to a Muslim/Croat population of about 10.000. Finally, we will present the testimony of Dr. Ewa Tabeau, an expert in the field of demographics, and she will present data relating to the demographic changes in the 37 municipalities identified in our indictment. I will not go into her statistics in my opening remarks, but I will say that they confirm the dramatic demographic reconfiguration of Bosnia. Now, if we could show the next exhibit, please. This map, prepared by OHR, shows the ethnic composition in Bosnia in 1998. And again, looking at the legend, you can see that the red colour represents predominantly Serb areas. Now, if we could have the previous map exhibited. Side by side, you have before you graphic evidence and an illustration of the effects of strategic objective number 1. Now, Your Honours, let me return to the indictment. And I'd like to focus on each of the counts in it, and focus on the accused's liability under Articles 7(1) and 7(3).

The same is true with the colour red, again decreasing from dark red, more than 66 per cent Serbs, to the lightest colour, Serbs up to 50 per cent. So we'll present that in a better form during the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the first two counts in the indictment charge genocide and complicity in genocide. In six municipalities, Bosanski Novi, Brcko, Kljuc, Kotor Varos, Prijedor, and Sanski Most, the campaign of persecutions included or escalated to include conduct committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, national, ethnic, racial, or religious groups, as such. In those municipalities, the killing of Bosnian Serb -- Muslims and Bosnian Croats, including leading members of those communities, occurred both during and after attacks on villages and towns, and in detention facilities. Our evidence will show that leading members of the non-Serb communities were targeted, and they and other members of those communities were detained in facilities under conditions of life calculated to bring about their physical destruction. Those conditions included physical and psychological abuse, torture, inadequate food, water, medical and hygienic conditions. The detention facilities themselves in those municipalities are listed in schedule C of the indictment, and they include the notorious facilities of the Luka Camp in Brcko, about which you will be hearing evidence immediately in this case, starting tomorrow; and the Omarska and Keraterm camps in the Prijedor municipality. Count 3 of the indictment charges persecutions, a crime against humanity, and it describes discriminatory acts that were directed against the Bosnian Muslims, the Bosnian Croats, and other non-Serbs in specific municipalities identified in the indictment. These persecutory acts were committed by Bosnian Serb political and governmental organs and by the Bosnian Serb and Serbian military, police, and paramilitaries. Paragraph 19 of the indictment identifies the various types of persecutory acts that were directed against the victims and the specific instances of those events are listed in the various schedules attached to the indictment. Now, in many of the municipalities identified in the indictment, a pattern emerged. That pattern was that the minority, the non-Serbs, were threatened, then they were disarmed by the Serb forces, and finally, they fell prey to the Serb forces, often with the assistance of the JNA and paramilitary formations. And through acts of murder, unlawful detention, and the like, they were expelled from their homes and their communities. The Muslim village of Glogova, in the municipality of Bratunac, is a classic example of this type of ethnic cleansing, and we will present evidence on the village of Glogova to you in this first block of days when we present this case to Your Honours. Now, the pervasive conduct and pattern by the Bosnian Serb governmental and police and paramilitary forces and their allies, disprove conclusively that these were random or spontaneous events. The acts described in paragraph 19 of the indictment were, instead, the fruition of a policy conceived of and promoted by the accused and others to remove permanently non-Serbs from the territory claimed by the Bosnian Serbs. Counts 4 to 6 charge the accused with two charges of crimes against humanity and the single count of the violations of the laws or customs of war. These charges describe killings of the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats and others that occurred during and after attacks on their settlements, and killings that occurred while these non-Serbs were unlawfully detained. The acts that support this part of the indictment are found in schedules A and B, and during the course of this trial, we will present evidence as to each of these acts. Finally, the remaining two counts in the indictment charge the accused with criminal responsibility for the forcible transfer and deportation of non-Serbs from the municipalities that are identified in the indictment. These charges reflect one of the desired objectives of the Bosnian Serb forces. Now, let me turn my attention to the criminal responsibility of the accused under Article 7(1). We have charged Mr. Krajisnik with criminal responsibility for the crimes enumerated in the indictment because of his role in planning, instigating, ordering, committing, or aiding and abetting in the preparation and execution of them. Our evidence will be presented to Your Honours throughout the course of the trial, and I will not detail it here. But I would like to focus for a few minutes your attention on the allegation that he's criminally responsible for committing the crimes in the indictment because of his participation in a joint criminal enterprise. As I said, the word "committing" in this indictment doesn't mean that Momcilo Krajisnik personally shot or beat people or that he personally torched a house or that he destroyed a mosque. People at his level rarely do. Others do it for them. The term "committed" in this case refers exclusively to his participation in the criminal enterprise, the objective of which I have said many times. Now, I have earlier shown you a map reflecting the ethnic make-up of Bosnia before the war, and I'd like to return to it for just a minute. And if we could have it on the screen. This is the map showing the areas where Bosnian Serbs lived, both in Croatia and in Bosnia, and you will see again from that map it depicts the ethnic populations and their concentrations in Bosnia. As you'll see at a closer look - and thank you, Ms. Javier for showing us this - the darkest blue areas represent the highest concentration of Serb populations, and you will see that going down to the white areas where there are virtually none. And it's been said oftentimes that a map of Bosnia before the war showing the ethnic populations and their distribution resemble the hide of a leopard. Looking at this map today in this courtroom, it's clear to us, as it was clear to Mr. Krajisnik before the war, as he was a native of Bosnia, when he implemented his division for a divided Bosnia, that the physical separation of ethnic communities in Bosnia would not be possible. People simply would not agree voluntarily to abandon their age-old hearths to satisfy the political goals and objectives of the Bosnian Serbs. Yet the physical separation and permanent removal of Muslims and Croats from the Serbian-claimed territory was precisely a policy of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Now, each member of the joint criminal enterprise contributed in different ways to achieving the objectives of the enterprise, and throughout this trial, you will hear evidence about the contributions of Radovan Karadzic, Ratko Mladic, Biljana Plavsic, Arkan, General Talic, Radoslav Brdjanin, and other members of the enterprise. I've already mentioned many of the accused's contributions to the joint criminal enterprise. His central role in the creation and in the implementation of Bosnian Serb policies of the Bosnian Serbs, his vital role in the creation of the Bosnian Serb army, one of the principal instruments used in the cleansing operations; his role in the selection of Ratko Mladic as the commander of the Bosnian Serb army and his role in the creation of the variant A and variant B instructions. We intend to present considerable evidence about his other contributions to this criminal enterprise throughout this trial. But let me focus for a few minutes on his crucial role in the creation of Bosnian Serb policy, specifically on the strategic objectives that I've previously discussed. Our evidence in this trial will show that Momcilo Krajisnik was instrumental in formulating these objectives. As Karadzic said when announcing this particular objective, the first objective, in all of the objectives, I should say - I should correct myself - it was formulated "by the presidency, the government, the Council for National Security." Council for National Security, the accused was a member of that. And indeed, the accused himself underscored the importance in his role in formulating the objectives at the same session when they were announced. I will use his words. According to Momcilo Krajisnik: "As for the strategic goals, I would like to offer an explanation, since I have also taken part in adopting these goals. We must make a choice regarding one thing. The first goal is the most important one, and in relation to all other goals, all other goals are subitems to the first one." Now, our evidence that we will present during the course of this trial will show that Momcilo Krajisnik was an ardent and a persistent proponent of the concept of ethnic division of the Muslims and the Croats at the 11th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, approximately two months before the strategic objectives were formally announced, Momcilo Krajisnik said, when discussing the progress of international efforts to find solutions to the Yugoslav crisis, and let me quote again Mr. Krajisnik: "I think the problem is that they want Bosnia and Herzegovina to internationally recognised at any cost. They want it to be a state. In this respect, it would be good if we could do one thing for strategic reasons: If we could start implementing what we have agreed upon, the ethnic division on the ground. That we start determining the territory at once, and once the territory is determined, it remains to be established for additional negotiations whose authorities are to function and in what way. I cannot say whether this will be fair in political terms. There is not much fairness in politics, after all. And yes, if it does not turn out to be fair, the Serbian people will be blamed. But we cannot accept a state designed in the mind of the SDA people." Now, our evidence in the course of this trial will show that Mr. Krajisnik persisted to hold firmly to the view that the territory of the Bosnian Serbs must be clean, and we will introduce evidence to this effect during this trial. Now, our indictment alleges alternatively that the crimes enumerated in the counts in the indictment were the natural and foreseeable consequences of the execution of the joint criminal enterprise, and that Momcilo Krajisnik was aware that these crimes were the possible consequence of the execution of it. Now, was it foreseeable that the effort to forcibly separate Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the homes on which they had lived -- and in which they had lived for generations and for centuries, would result in the types of crimes that are described in the indictment? Was it foreseeable that the crimes contained in the indictment would be perpetrated against non-Serbs by Bosnian Serb forces in order to achieve self-contained territories? The answer again to both questions is a resounding yes. At the 4th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, presided over by Momcilo Krajisnik, Radovan Karadzic predicted what would occur if Bosnia and Herzegovina was to become independent. He predicted a civil war and he predicted its consequences. I quote: "Apart from causing the deaths of several hundred thousand people and complete destruction of several hundred towns, a civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina would also result in massive and rapid population movements; in other words, it would lead to population homogenisation." At the 10th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, again presided over by the accused, Karadzic repeated, virtually verbatim, these same words. His grim prediction echoes his earlier threat on the 14th of October, 1991, and we saw a film clip of Mr. Karadzic earlier threatening the Muslims with the prospect of disappearing. His grim predictions are reflected in the threat on the 14th of October, 1991. Now, when the strategic objectives were publicly announced at the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992, the Bosnian Serb deputies in attendance understood precisely their meaning. Our evidence will show this to be the case. Listen to the words uttered by the representative from Bosanska Krupa, Miroslav Vjestica, who was also the SDS president of the municipal board from Bosanska Krupa and would, in 1995, become the vice-president of the Republika Srpska government in charge of internal affairs. And I should add parenthetically that Bosanska Krupa is one of the municipalities about which you will here evidence during the course of this trial. According to Mr. Vjestica, and I quote: "I give my full consent to all the strategic goals that have been proposed." He goes on to say: "What have we done in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa? I must tell you -- I must remind you that there is only 24 per cent of Serbs in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. There is 14.500 of us, and there is 47.000 Muslims." He then goes on to say: "For a year and a half we have been preparing for the war in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa because we knew that we would be at war and it cannot be avoided." He goes on further to say: "How could it happen that two-thirds of the town were taken in two days of operations? Thank God we did get to our borders, because that is how we envisioned them and drawn them and you, people's deputies, know well that that we had said that the right bank of the Una would be our border and that the right bank of the Una River must be the border, after all, the natural border of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina runs from Bihac via Bosanska Krupa to Bosanski Novi. That was what we claimed, and that was why we did get to the right bank of the Una River." Finally, he says in his speech: "On the right bank of the Una River there are no more Muslims in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. All the enclaves that were there" - and he lists those enclaves - "we have evacuated them so that there will be none there for the duration of war operations. Will they have a place to return to? I think it is unlikely after our president told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una River was the border." As I say, Your Honours will hear considerable evidence about what happened in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. Listen to the words of Dragan Kalinic from the municipality of Sarajevo, and I quote him: "We have chosen the option of war or the option of negotiation. I say this with reason, and I must instantly add that, knowing who our enemy is, how perfidious they are, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically, militarily destroyed and crushed, which of course implies eliminating their key people. I do not hesitate in selecting the first option, the option of war. The fate of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot be solved in any other way but by war." Our evidence will show, Your Honours, that the events on the ground conclusively demonstrate that the meaning of the first strategic objective was clearly understood before its formal announcement on the 12th of May. To give you briefly some examples: In the Brcko municipality, about which you'll hear evidence starting tomorrow, Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat civilians were rounded up and detained in the notorious camp, the Luka camp. Again, before the announcement of these objectives, in the Bratunac municipality, about which you'll hear evidence at this session, the village of Glogova was attacked, it was torched, and its entire Muslim population removed. In the Bosanski Novi municipality, which is the third municipality in succession, about which you'll hear evidence, not this session but the next, Bosnian Muslim civilians were arrested, placed on trains, and forcibly removed from the municipality. I won't go further, Your Honours, but I'd like to turn now to Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal and the responsibility of Momcilo Krajisnik for the crimes described in the indictment under that particular article. The law is clear that to be criminally responsible under 7(3), the accused may either be a civilian or a military superior, and in order to establish criminal liability under Article 7(3), it's incumbent on the Prosecution to establish that an offence was committed, that the accused exercised superior authority over the perpetrators of the offence, that he knew or had reason to know that a subordinate was about to commit a crime or had done so, and that he had failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the offence from occurring or from punishing the perpetrators. Now, the first of these elements, that the offences occurred during the course of the period of the indictment, was repeatedly denied by the Bosnian Serb leadership as they were occurring, and our evidence will demonstrate beyond a reasonable doubt the contrary. The second element, superior authority over the perpetrators of the offence, requires that a superior/subordinate relationship must have existed between the accused and the perpetrator at the relevant time. Our Tribunal has defined this to mean a superior must have effective control over persons committing the underlying offences, in the sense of having the material ability to prevent and punish the commission of these offences. The evidence that we will present during the course of this trial will show Your Honours that Momcilo Krajisnik had both de facto and de jure control over the perpetrators of the offences described in the indictment. Turning my attention first of all to the evidence on the issue of Krajisnik's effective control, the following factors may be relevant to a finding by this Trial Chamber of effective control by a superior over de facto subordinates. These factors, which I will quickly run through, are factors that have been recognised by the jurisprudence in this institution. They include, but they are not limited to: The capacity to sign orders; the substance of those orders; whether the orders were acted upon; the position of the accused in the overall institutional, political, and military organisations; the actual tasks performed; the evidence that the accused has a high political profile; the accused's overall behaviour towards subordinates and his duties; the accused's use of his extant authority to prevent crimes and mistreatment; the exercise of powers generally attached to a military command; the submitting of reports to competent authorities in order for proper measures to be taken; and finally, sanctioning power. These are a list of some of the elements that Your Honours can consider. Now, our evidence that we will present during the course of this trial will show plainly that Momcilo Krajisnik indeed had effective control over the forces that committed the crimes alleged in the indictment. His position in the SDS party, including being a member of the Main Board and a member of the commission for personnel, vested him with vast powers and influence. In the government structures of the Bosnian Serb entity, he held numerous formal positions at the apex of power, including being a member of the National Security Council. This wasn't merely an advisory body, but it acted as a de facto presidency and exercised powers of that office during the time period when Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic were the acting presidents of the Bosnian Serb Republic, in other words, in the chart that I had previously shown, during the time period when those two individuals at the top of the chart were members of the acting presidency. Later, Momcilo Krajisnik became a member of the expanded presidency, a body that was the supreme commander of the army and which had plenary authority over the police. He was also the speaker of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the most elevated position in that body. And he was the head of War Commissions. In addition, he was often selected to represent the Bosnian Serb Republic in international conferences and negotiations. Now, in addition to his party positions in the SDS, in addition to his official government positions, he maintained a close working relationship with Radovan Karadzic, Slobodan Milosevic, General Ratko Mladic, and other political and military figures. This will be reflected in considerable evidence that we present to Your Honours during the course of this trial, but I'd like to play just one example of that for Your Honours. It is an intercept of a telephone conversation between the accused and Ratko Mladic on the 27th of May, 1992. And, Your Honours, I have instructed -- I've requested from Your Honours whether or not it is necessary to have these simultaneously translated. I've been informed it is not, and I've informed the booth of the position of the Trial Chamber. So there will be no simultaneous translation, and you will be able to listen to the words, the tone of this conversation, and you'll be able to read the script without interruption. So if that could be played, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That concludes the intercept. Now, because of these official positions and his close relationships with Karadzic, Mladic, and other members of the joint criminal enterprise, our evidence will establish beyond a reasonable doubt his effective control over the Bosnian Serb political institutions, as well as the military police and associated forces that were indispensable to achieving the Bosnian Serb objectives. Now, earlier in my remarks I mentioned that the accused was a member of the expanded presidency. His de jure authority over the perpetrators of the crimes, some of the crimes identified in the indictment, emanated from this position. He served in this capacity from the 2nd of June until the 17th of December, 1992. Now, after the constitution of the Bosnian Serb Republic was promulgated, the most important executive organ through which the Bosnian Serb leadership exercised its power was the office of the president of the Republic. However, this position remained unoccupied until the 17th of December, 1992, when Radovan Karadzic was elected to that position. One of the vital powers conferred on the president by the constitution was to command the army, to appoint and dismiss its officers, and the evidence that we will present will show that before Karadzic finally became the president on the 17th of December, 1992, interim collective presidencies discharged the function of the president. In this respect, one of the collective presidency members, acting on behalf of the presidency, commanded the army and appointed and promoted and dismissed officers. I have to emphasise that the collective presidencies, in their various iterations, were precisely that: Collective decision-making bodies, and decisions were taken after consultations within the collective body. Indeed, Your Honours, the accused firmly believed in the collective decision-making process. This is what he said: "I believe that it is normal to have centralisation of authority in the war, but I would always be in favour of the idea not to concentrate the power in the hands of only one man, starting from myself, and then everybody else. Mr. Karadzic is not a controlling man and he doesn't even want the power, but I would promote that there is a consciousness in each and every one of us. Mr. Karadzic feels the same way. He is in favour of leadership of Serbian people, instead of its leader. Because when you have leadership, then you have more common sense, more heads, so to speak, and the decisions are of much better quality than they would be if they were made only by one man. In order for us to be efficient, we must have unanimous decisions. We must work as one. And if there's any one of us missing, a different opinion is immediately created. I mean, conflict about something, that is normal. That is why it's needed to have more engagement, and I would personally promote the presidency and not the president, especially since they are all people of great quality. They are all very patriotic, and it would be a pity to eliminate some of them and leave only one to make all the decisions. And honestly, the responsibility in the war is great and it is necessary to share the responsibility." So those were Mr. Krajisnik's views before he became a member of the presidency. Now, our evidence that we will present to Your Honours will show that the presidency issued numerous orders, including, in some instances, direct combat orders to the army. For example, in the minutes of the 12th session of the presidency, they reflect that the presidency ordered the Bosnian Serb army to "immediately cease all artillery and infantry operations in the suburbs of Dobrinja," and further ordered that the Bosnian Serb army move from offensive to defensive positions. Now, what was the essence of the presidency's command authority over the army? Our evidence will show that the law on the army - we'll introduce the law of the army to Your Honours - emphasised that the exercise of command was founded on the principle of unity of command and the obligation to exercise -- to execute, I'm sorry, the decisions, commands, and orders of superiors. This fundamental principle was acknowledged in one of the military reports that we will introduce into evidence. It says, in part: "The Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will continue to implement, resolutely and uncompromisingly, the decisions of the state and political leadership of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, similarly, the presidency had direct command over the police. We'll present evidence to Your Honours to that effect. Under Article 7(3), to prove criminal responsibility, it's incumbent on the Office of the Prosecutor to prove that the accused knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit crimes or had done so. Let me focus a bit on the evidence that Momcilo Krajisnik had reason to know that his subordinates were about to or had committed crimes. From the minutes of the various Bosnian Serb assemblies, over which Mr. Krajisnik presided as its president, he knew that if a political solution was not found on the issue of sovereignty to Bosnia, war would ensue and the Serb forces would unleash the dogs of war in order to achieve their overriding objectives of creating a Serb state. Throughout the debates which the accused attended, the crimes in this indictment were forecast repeatedly. Let me take you to the 4th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, on the 21st of December, 1991. Listen to the words of Assemblyman Vukic: "If the European Community goes on with its threat to recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state," he sets the stage, he goes on to say: "There will be massive bloodshed in which nations that have been subsequently created will disappear altogether." That's very reminiscent of what Mr. Karadzic said in his famous speech about disappearing and in his subsequent speeches about war resulting in hundreds of thousands of deaths, destroyed homes, and massive and bloody, forcible dislocation of minorities. At the 12th Assembly session, Assemblyman Kozic said, and I quote: "The enemy, Ustashas and Mujahedin, has to be defeated by whatever means are necessary and only after that can we negotiate." Milenko Vojinovic, also known as Dr. Beli, from the Brcko municipality about which you'll hear tomorrow, said at the 16th assembly of the Serb Assembly on the 12th of May, in speaking about Brcko requiring more forces, he said they needed those forces "for a definitive clearing of the area." Now, by implementing a policy to separate the Serbs from the non-Serbs on the territory coveted by the Serbs, our evidence will show that Momcilo Krajisnik knew that the direction he was leading the Bosnian Serb people and he knew that these would lead to the commission of massive crimes. One of the groups that was responsible for those crimes, paramilitary groups -- I discussed earlier the events in Bijeljina, the actions of Arkan, who wasn't alone. He wasn't the only paramilitary in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Momcilo Krajisnik was fully apprised of the types of people who filled the ranks of the paramilitary units. He received clear notice of it. In a remarkably candid report prepared by the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb army, dated the 28th of July, 1992, and entitled "Report on paramilitary formations in the territory of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and distributed to, amongst others, the president of the Bosnian -- the president of the presidency, the prime minister, the VRS Main Staff commander. The main characteristics of those paramilitary units is described. And I have extracted certain of those descriptions from that report that we will lead into evidence: "They are mainly composed of individuals of low moral quality, and in many cases, of persons previously prosecuted for crimes and offences, and even convicted for crimes of murder, robbery, larceny, and the like. Very often, such units have in their ranks pathological criminals whom the conditions of war and general lawlessness have brought to the fore." In another part of the report, it says: "Many formations of this type display hatred of non-Serbian peoples, and one can conclude without reservation that they are the genocidal element among the Serbian people." The report states further: "War profiteering and looting are the motive for the great majority of paramilitaries." It goes on finally, in the last extract I've taken from that report, reads as follows: "One feature common to all paramilitary formations is that they do not take part in direct fighting with the enemy. Instead, they are operating behind the lines of the regular Serbian Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina army units, looting and burning property and killing the innocent population, or, as our people say, stealing chickens." Now, this report that we will lead into evidence identifies by name many of the units responsible for the predations on the non-Serb civilians. You'll hear testimonies from the victims of these paramilitary groups. Some of the paramilitary groups identified in this report you already know. The Arkanovci, headed by Arkan. I've described for you briefly some of his actions in Bijeljina. The Seseljovci, the paramilitary group under the leadership of Vojislav Seselj, who is currently awaiting trial in this institution. But this report also identified lesser-known paramilitary groups who were involved in the crimes throughout these municipalities. Now, you're going to hear evidence that there were orders issued to integrate these paramilitary groups into the Bosnian Serb army or disband them, and indeed, many of the important paramilitary groups identified in this report were incorporated into the Bosnian Serb army. Momcilo Krajisnik promoted the incorporation of these elements into the Bosnian Serb army. Now, there are many examples that you will hear throughout this trial of these paramilitary groups being incorporated into the army, but let me tell you about one such group, a smaller group, a lesser-known group. It hailed from the municipality of Prnjavor, which again is one of the municipalities about which you will hear evidence and hear the victims. The commander of that group was a man by the name of Veljko Milankovic. He was a man who had been prosecuted seven times, and he had been brought before the misdemeanour court 17 times. The paramilitary group that he led consisted of 150 men. According to the Main Staff report, Milankovic's group "is, as of recently, formally under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps." The report goes on to say, and I quote: "Members of this detachment are involved in extensive looting." And as Your Honours know, looting forms part of this indictment. Now, despite direct knowledge of the ongoing illegal conduct of this unit, it remained part of the corps structure, and moreover, Milankovic, whose unsavoury record I've described, remained an officer in that unit until his death, at which time he was later recommended for a posthumous decoration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I'm looking at the clock. It's close to 7.00. Could you find a suitable moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will. Now, did the presidency have clear and direct notice of these -- that these elements within the army were committing these foul deeds? Our evidence will show that they did. Our evidence will show that perhaps a few of these units were purged, but by and large they were not. Our evidence will show that perhaps a few members of these units were prosecuted, but the majority were not. These unsavoury elements remained in the Bosnian Serb army and the political leadership used these elements to achieve their political goals. And this, Your Honour, is a perfect time to break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I've got one question for you: How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would say no more than half an hour tomorrow morning, or tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, tomorrow in the afternoon. Then could the Chamber receive a short list of all the exhibits shown to the -- which I do understand that most of them will be tendered into evidence, so that we can -- we at least know what the proper identification of what exactly it was, whether we saw the whole, whether we saw part of certain documents, so that we can keep track of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is no problem, and tomorrow I will present that to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there will be a technical way of -- some of the pictures we saw, of course some parts were enlarged, but sometimes the whole of the picture was very difficult to see on the screen. Sometimes when it was blue I even thought I was looking at a Rorschach test rather than at a map. So if we could find a way of at least using a full screen for these pictures, that would be nice. Madam Registrar, we will sit tomorrow on from a quarter past 2.00 in courtroom -- in this same courtroom? Yes. Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of February 2004, at 2.15 p.m.
